title: How to Use a Family Catechism
excerpt: A catechism is not a test. It is a set of true sentences, learned by heart in childhood, that surface decades later when a person needs them most.
body:
The word catechism scares people who did not grow up with it. It sounds severe, like memorization for its own sake, like faith reduced to flashcards. That is a misunderstanding worth clearing away, because a catechism is one of the most loving things a parent can hand a child, and almost no one uses it anymore.

A catechism is simply a list of the most important questions a human being can ask, paired with true and careful answers, written to be learned by heart. "What is your only comfort in life and in death?" "Who made you?" "What is the chief end of man?" These are not trivia. They are the questions your child will face whether or not anyone prepared them, and a catechism prepares them.

## Why memory matters more than feeling

We live downstream of a long suspicion of rote learning. We were told that anything memorized is dead, that real faith must be felt and discovered rather than received. There is a half-truth in that and a great lie underneath it.

The lie is that a person can summon true words in a crisis that they never put into their memory in calm. They cannot. The night a man stands at a graveside, he does not invent a theology of death on the spot. He reaches for what is already in him. If "What is your only comfort in life and in death? That I am not my own, but belong to my faithful Savior Jesus Christ" is already lodged in his memory from childhood, it is there to reach for. If it was never put there, the reaching comes up empty.

You are not loading your child with dead words. You are stocking a cellar against a winter you cannot predict.

## How to actually do it

Pick one catechism and stay with it. The Heidelberg Catechism is warm and pastoral. The Westminster Shorter Catechism is precise and weighty. There are children's versions written in plain language for the very young. Any of them will serve. The mistake is to keep shopping for the perfect one instead of starting the available one.

Do one question at a time, and do not rush. A single question and answer per week is plenty for a young child. Say it together at the same moment every day, most easily attached to a meal you already share. You say the question. The whole family says the answer. That is the entire method.

Review the old ones as you add new ones, so that by the end of a year a child holds fifty true sentences in their bones. Children memorize without effort what adults strain to retain. Use the years while that gift is strong.

## Explain, but do not over-explain

A catechism is meant to be understood eventually, not immediately. A four-year-old can say "God made me and all things" long before they grasp what made means. That is fine. The words go in first; the understanding fills them later, the way a riverbed is dug before the river comes.

When a child asks what an answer means, say a sentence, not a lecture. "Belong means we are his, and he takes care of what is his." Then move on. The questions will deepen as they age. Save the long answers for the long questions that are coming.

I have watched a child rattle off a catechism answer with no apparent comprehension, and then, two years later, ask a question about that very line that stopped me cold. The words were waiting in them for the day they would mean something. That is exactly how it is supposed to work.

## Do not make it a battle

If catechism becomes a fight, you have lost the point. It is not a performance to be graded. A child who is tired or distracted can listen while the others recite. A child who gets it wrong is simply corrected gently and moved past. The aim is a household where these sentences are common air, repeated until they are no longer remarkable, the way a child knows the words to a song they cannot remember learning.

## This week

Choose one catechism and find its first question. Read it aloud at dinner tonight and have everyone say the answer together. Do the same one every day this week until the youngest can say it without prompting. Next week, add the second, and review the first. Keep a small card on the table so no one has to hunt for it.

In a year you will have given your children something the culture cannot give them and cannot take away. A set of true words, learned before they were needed, ready for the day they will be.
